title: Errors as values: the `error` interface and the handling idiom

videos.script: Lesson 31 finished generics. This lesson is about what a program does when something goes wrong. {{value}} In Go, a failure is not thrown. It comes back from the function as a value, beside the result, and the caller looks at it on the next line. Its type is an interface with one method, and nil means nothing failed. {{idiom}} Then the line you will type more than any other in Go: if err is not nil. You will run it against a missing file and a number that is not a number. And the ticket price from lesson 19, which said minus one for a bad age, gets an error instead. {{ignore}} You will also see what happens when the error is thrown away. The program carries on, and sells a free ticket to somebody aged thirty. {{custom}} Last, an error type of your own, which carries the line where the input went wrong. And one trap the compiler does not catch. An error holding a nil pointer is not nil, so the program reports a failure and prints nil as the reason. {{nil}} By the end you can read any Go function that can fail, and write one.
